<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
The comment does two different things, and they deserve different verdicts:

- **Sections 1–4 are strong.** They use microdata to document problems the working paper understated, and they confirm several concerns I raised about Halden: the withdrawals, the manager-completed index, the scheduled-hours denominator, and nominal revenue.
- **Sections 6–8 overreach.** The conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" isn't supported by the comment's own numbers. It also requires setting aside the one randomised positive result in the literature.

It mirrors the Halden paper's error in the opposite direction: a good critique of an overclaim becomes an overclaimed null.

## Arithmetic

Table 2 checks out:
- 98.7 / 0.8 gives +23.4%.
- 95.1 / 0.8 gives +18.9%.
- 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, and 98.4 / 0.859 gives +14.6%.
- 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861, and 95.4 / 0.861 gives +10.8%.

The real-revenue figure checks out: 1.014 / 1.041 ≈ −2.6%.

**One thing doesn't reconcile: the hours decomposition in Section 3.** With 32 scheduled hours over four days, +0.7 hours per day adds 2.8 and 1.6 hours on the day off adds more. That gives about 36.4 hours, not 34.6. If the +0.7 is measured against baseline days of about 8.06 hours, it's worse, about 36.6. For the components to sum to 34.6, the extension of the four days would have to be about +0.25 hours, not +0.7.

Possible explanations:
- The +0.7 figure comes from a different subset.
- It's unweighted while the total is weighted.
- It includes the 17 organisations with staggered schedules differently.

The authors need to fix this or explain it. It's the paper's own evidence for the hours correction.

## Strengths

**The attrition finding is the most important contribution.** If seven of nine withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule began, and six cited workload or output, then the working paper's "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons" is a material misstatement. That's more than a limitation. The Halden authors should correct it. (A small point: 6 + 2 = 8, so the ninth exit reason is missing.)

**Section 2's manager vs records comparison is persuasive.** The manager index exceeded the records in 19 of 23 organisations. A sign test gives p ≈ 0.003, so the direction is not chance. The authors are also careful not to allege bad faith.

**The revenue deflation is correct**, and so is the observation that per-hour metrics turn any output above 80 into a "gain."

**The recommendations** (record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up, intention-to-treat including withdrawals) are right.

## Problems

### 1. The abstract claims a correction the analysis didn't make

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems brings the gain to 10.8%. The first three problems listed are attrition, output measure, and hours. **Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition isn't adjusted for anywhere.** The 10.8% is a survivors-only figure, which the authors acknowledge in Section 6.

A bounding exercise would show how much attrition matters. Suppose the nine withdrawals had output of 80, i.e. zero per-hour gain. Weighting by organisation, the headline output becomes roughly (61 × 98.7 + 9 × 80) / 70 ≈ 96.3, about +20% per scheduled hour. On that rough check, attrition is real but probably not the largest of the four problems. Lee bounds or a worst-case imputation would make this precise.

### 2. The 23.4% → 10.8% comparison mixes samples

The 23.4% covers all 61 organisations. The 10.8% covers 17 organisations that kept both records and time tracking. Part of the drop could be composition: those 17 may differ from the rest. The clean decomposition starts from the *as-reported* figure for the same 17, then applies each correction. The data note concedes the subset problem, but the abstract and conclusion present the before and after as like for like.

The table also doesn't say whether the means are employee-weighted, as Halden's were, or unweighted. That changes comparability.

### 3. "Billable hours delivered" is an input, not an output

Professional services make up the largest Halden sector. For them, a record-based "output" of billable hours falls mechanically when hours are cut. Using it as output biases the record-based index downward and pushes the per-hour gain toward zero by construction.

The authors should:
- report Section 2 and the 17-organisation estimate separately by record type, and
- check the result without organisations whose records are billable hours.

### 4. No uncertainty on any re-estimate

The 10.8% rests on 17 organisations and has no confidence interval. Given the spread across organisations, the interval will be wide. Without it, the reader can't tell whether the residual differs from zero, which is exactly what the conclusion asserts.

### 5. The novelty argument uses the wrong variable and ignores the right one

The comment links the residual output gain to a decline in self-reported **energy**, extrapolated linearly from two points (0.61 → 0.29) to reach zero "around month ten." Linear extrapolation actually gives about month 8.7, but two points can't distinguish a decline from a decline that levels off.

More importantly, **Halden collected the output index monthly, and the authors have the microdata.** The direct test of a novelty effect is whether output per actual hour declined across months one to six in the 17-organisation subset. The comment doesn't report it. Until it does, novelty is a hypothesis, not a correction. "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" can't turn an untested alternative into a finding of zero.

### 6. The Varden trial is cited selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." That's an overstatement, since it rests on 5 v 5 clusters with possibly too-narrow confidence intervals. More importantly, the comment ignores the other Varden stratum. In case-processing, the same trial found:

- **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4).**
- This used administrative records and timesheet hours, against a randomised control, measured at nine months.

That is a per-hour gain with all three of the comment's concerns addressed by design: measurement, selection and the hours denominator. Its timing, nine months, is beyond the comment's own estimate of when novelty would have faded. "Entirely an artifact" can't stand alongside it without engaging it.

### 7. The meetings hypothesis is misdescribed

The comment says the Varden meetings analysis was "selected for analysis after the results were known." By the trial's own account:
- the data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results;
- the analysis was labelled exploratory and unregistered;
- it was explicitly said not to establish a mechanism;
- a confirmatory test was registered for the 24-month follow-up.

The Varden authors already said what the comment says. They didn't "cite it as a mechanism."

The meetings data also bear on novelty in a way the comment misses. On a rough level comparison, treated case-processing staff had about 29 non-meeting hours a week against about 31 in control. That implies most of the per-hour gain could be removed meeting time. If confirmed, that would be a structural gain, which is exactly what a novelty account can't explain.

### 8. The conclusion contradicts the paper's own results

The comment's own best estimate is about **+11%**, in a non-random subset, with an untested decay story. The best randomised evidence shows **+12.5%** in non-coverage work. "Entirely an artifact" is a much stronger claim than either supports.

The hedge "in our assessment" doesn't fix this. The defensible conclusion is roughly:

> The Halden pilot overstated the per-hour gain by more than half. After correcting output and hours in the subset where this is possible, a gain of roughly 11% remains, whose durability is untested. Randomised evidence suggests gains of similar size in work not tied to presence, possibly driven partly by meeting reduction, and clear losses in coverage-bound work.

## Summary of what I'd ask the authors to do

1. Reconcile the hours decomposition in Section 3.
2. Remove "correcting the first three" from the abstract, or add an attrition correction (bounds or imputation).
3. Do the decomposition within the 17-organisation subset, starting from its own as-reported figure, and state the weighting.
4. Separate billable-hours records from true output records.
5. Report confidence intervals on all re-estimates.
6. Test novelty directly using the monthly output data.
7. Engage the Varden case-processing result and describe the meetings analysis accurately.
8. Revise the conclusion to match the evidence.

Across the three papers, the evidence points to one picture:
- **Coverage-bound work:** reduced hours reduce output.
- **Queue-based work:** real but modest per-hour gains, probably 10–13%, mechanism uncertain, with meeting reduction a plausible part.
- **Halden's headline:** about twice too large.

None of the three papers states this picture; each overclaims in one direction or the other. If you'd like, I could write the synthesis note setting it out.
